clue: Dollars in the top prize Regis dangled
reason: The dollars are the counted thing and the clue names them exactly; the trivia hook is fair garnish.

clue: The jackpot Regis dangled
reason: Names the prize object associated with the number instead of the dollars it counts — the jackpot is not itself a number.

clue: Orange eye winking in the ash long after the flames give up
reason: A precise sensory scene of the ordinary sense — the picture is the clue

clue: Small piece of burning coal or wood
reason: Dictionary gloss verbatim — accurate, economical, and utterly without a picture

clue: Grass that can grow three feet in a single day
reason: Two checkable surprises in one line — it's a grass, and the growth rate astonishes

clue: Plant that pandas eat
reason: The single most recycled association for the answer, delivered without lift

clue: Only bird that can fly backward
reason: Specific, checkable, and genuinely remark-worthy — 'only' is earned here, not an overclaim

clue: Tiny bird that sips nectar
reason: True and dull — the stock description any solver could produce unprompted

clue: Device that turns 6 A.M. into a crime scene
reason: Fresh comic image with its own energy — enjoyable as a line even if the answer were blank

clue: Handy clock feature that gets you up in the morning!
reason: Chirpy register substituting for humor — nothing here a dictionary entry couldn't have said

clue: Tree whose winged seeds helicopter down
reason: True and vividly put; also fits ASH or ELM, which is fine — crossings do the disambiguating

clue: Only tree whose sap can be boiled into syrup
reason: The flaw is falsity, not breadth — birch sap makes syrup too, so 'only' overclaims

clue: Dome built from what it keeps out
reason: Every word carries the paradox that defines the thing; nothing is removable without losing the definition.

clue: Dome built from blocks of frozen snow
reason: 'frozen' is padding — snow is frozen by definition, and its deletion leaves the clue just as complete and precise.

clue: Reason to spike the ball?
reason: The ? marks definition-by-consequence, and the metonymy reads true — the event is exactly why the ball gets spiked.

clue: Six points?
reason: Equates the event with its score — it earns six points but is not six points; the ? cannot repair a false equivalence.

clue: One rolling in dough?
reason: The wealth idiom points away while the literal rolling-of-dough is true of the answer — a textbook earned ?.

clue: Bread professional?
reason: Flat occupational fact under an unearned ? — no figurative reading exists for the mark to signal.

clue: Shawls and stoles
reason: The outer-garment sense stands on its own — a legitimate secondary meaning, no idiom required.

clue: Secrecy?
reason: The secrecy sense lives only inside 'under wraps' — the word alone never means it, and no ? repairs a sense we don't own.

clue: Claw-backed tool for driving nails
reason: Both qualifiers hold — the claw and the nail-driving are literal features of the common form

clue: The only tool that can drive a nail
reason: 'Only' overclaims — mallets and nail guns drive nails too; strip the false exclusivity

clue: Spiny desert plant that stores water in its stem
reason: Each qualifier — spiny, desert, stem-stored water — is literally true and jointly pins

clue: Desert plant that never needs water
reason: 'Never' overclaims — the plant famously needs little water, but the absolute makes the clue false

clue: Wall dial nudged upward when the living room turns chilly
reason: The nudging is what you do to the answer and only the answer; the domestic moment is doing definitional work.

clue: Glass column whose silver thread climbs with the fever
reason: A climbing mercury thread is a thermometer — the measuring neighbor, not the controlling device the answer names.

clue: Sagging web slung between two trees and occupied all afternoon
reason: The slung-between-trees detail pins the referent uniquely; the lazy-afternoon image is definitional color, not padding.

clue: Folding canvas seat hauled out for an afternoon nap on the deck
reason: Folding and hauled-out define a deck chair; the answer is hung, not unfolded — the scene fits the neighbor.
